fields.title: Food perception liver phosphoproteome induced by caged food and POMC neuron activation
fields.description: Liver mitochondria play a central role in metabolic adaptations to changing nutritional states, yet their dynamic regulation upon anticipated changes in energy state has remained unaddressed. Here, we show that sensory food perception rapidly induces mitochondrial fission in the liver via protein kinase B/AKT-dependent phosphorylation of serine 131 of the Mitochondrial fission factor (MFFS131), and this response is mediated via activation of hypothalamic Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons. A non-phosphorylatable MFFS131G knock-in mutation abrogates AKT-induced mitochondrial fragmentation in vitro. In vivo, MFFS131G knock-in mice display altered liver mitochondrial dynamics upon food perception and refeeding and impaired insulin stimulated suppression of gluconeogenesis. Collectively, we reveal a critical role for rapid activation of a hypothalamic/liver axis to adapt mitochondrial function to anticipated changes of nutritional state in control of hepatic glucose metabolism.   The repository contains two LC-MS/MS datasets aiming for the detection of phosphorylated peptides. a) POMC neuron activation and b) time course experiment of fasted, refed and caged food. We assumed that due to the short time (30 min max) that the total protein level remain unchanged.
fields.sample_protocol: In vivo optogenetic photostimulation (POMC activation) Following bilateral virus injection and optical fiber implantation, mice were allowed a post-surgical recovery period of 3 weeks. One week prior to experimental day, mice were habituated to a fiber-optic patch cord (core diameter 200 μm, numerical AP 0.48; Doric lenses) connected to a rotary joint (Doric lenses). On the day of experiment, at ZT 0, mice were fasted for 6 hours and new fiber-optic patch cords were attached. At ZT6 blue laser (473 nm) light stimulation consisting of pulse trains (5 ms pulses of 20 Hz; 3 s on, 1 s off) was delivered. A laser power of ~20 mW was employed. For phosphoproteomics of POMC activation, mice were sacrificed after 30 min.   Fasting, presentation of caged food, and refeeding (b)  Mice were fasted 2 hours after the beginning of the dark cycle (ZT 14) for 16 hours. On the following day at ZT6, mice were either exposed to caged food (inaccessible standard rodent chow that could be seen and smelled but not consumed) or were allowed to eat (refed) standard rodent chow (V1554, Ssniff) for the indicated timepoints.  Subcellular liver fractionation (b)  Whole livers were dissected, and washed 3 times in ice-cold Buffer 1 (225 mM mannitol, 75 mM sucrose and 30 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4)), minced, and washed again in 10 mL ice-cold Buffer 1 with a 40 μm Cell Strainer. Afterwards, liver pieces were homogenized in 5 mL of Buffer 2 (Buffer 1 supplemented with 0.5% (w/v) BSA A7030 Sigma, 0.5 mM EGTA and 1x Halt protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (PPIC) (78446, ThermoFisher)) with a rotating glass/Teflon Potter homogenizer (Potter S, Braun) using 12 strokes at 1,000 rpm. The homogenate was centrifuged at 400xg for 5 min at 4°C and the pellet homogenized again in 5 mL Buffer 2. Homogenates achieved from both homogenization steps were combined and a whole-homogenate sample was collected. The homogenate was centrifuged two times at 800xg for 5 min at 4°C to remove debris and nuclei. The resulting supernatant was centrifuged at 10,000xg and 4°C for 10 min to pellet a crude mitochondrial fraction. The crude mitochondria were then washed in 1 mL of Buffer 2 by centrifugation at 10,000xg and 4°C for 10 min. This washing step was repeated with 1 mL of Buffer 3 (440 mM Mannitol, 140 mM Sucrose, 10 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.4, 2 mM EGTA-KOH and 1x PPIC) and the pellet was snap frozen for phosphoproteomics in liver lysis buffer (Tris 50 mM, NaCl 130 mM, EDTA 5 mM, PMSF 100mM, NaF 100mM) if not used for isolation of pure mitochondria.  Protein Digestion and Phosphopeptide Enrichment  Liver (POMC activation) or crude mitochondrial lysates (fasted - refed/caged) were generated using a liver lysis buffer (Tris 50 mM, NaCl 130 mM, EDTA 5 mM, PMSF 100mM, NaF 100mM). A cOmplete Mini Protease Inhibitor Cocktail (1 tablet/10 mL, 1183617001, Roche) and 1% NP-40 were freshly added. Protein concentration was determined with a Pierce BCA Protein Assay Kit (23225, ThermoFisher), and 4000 µg protein were subjected for acetone precipitation (4x volume, -20°C overnight). The pellet was washed twice using ice-cold 85% acetone and dried for 5-10 min. 300 μL HEPES (100 mM pH=8.5) were added, and proteins were reduced using 10 mM TCEP for 15 min at 37°C and alkylated by 20 mM CAA for 45 min at 45°C. LysC (129-02541, FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corporation) mixture in 100 mM HEPES pH = 8.5 was added on the pellet in a 1:100 enzyme:substrate ratio and incubated for 2 hours at 37°C with 500 rpm. Trypsin (T6567, Sigma Aldrich) was then added and incubated overnight at 37°C on a ThermoMixer (shaking: 500 rpm). Generated peptides were desalted using the SepPak (Waters, 186000308, 50 mg sorbent).  Peptides were eluted using 80% acetonitrile and 0.1% formic acid. Samples were dried to complete dryness in a SpeedVac (Eppendorf Concentrator Plus).  Phosphorylated peptides were enriched using the HighSelect TiO2 Phosphopeptide enrichment Kit (A32993, Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacture’s protocol, using peptide equivalent to a total of 500-750 µg protein input (protein input within an experiment was equal). The eluate containing enriched p-sites was dried in a SpeedVac and resuspended in 8 µL 2% formic acid and 2.5% acetonitrile.
